- If sentiment is consistently neutral or negative over recent days, reduce forecasted price momentum; avoid over-optimistic spikes.
- When sentiment shows strong positive signals (e.g., >0.25), model should not over-forecast; cap upward revisions to avoid overshoot.
- If model forecasts a sharp upward move after a recent dip, check for mean reversion — often true price rebounds are muted or delayed.
- In cases of high sentiment volatility (e.g., alternating +1 and -1), model should smooth forecasts to avoid overreacting to short-term sentiment noise.
- If true outcome shows early mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 days after peak), model should reduce forecasted peak height and shift downward slope.
- For 30-day forecasts, if model consistently overpredicts by 1–2% in early days, apply a 0.5–1% downward adjustment to first 7–10 days.
- If sentiment history shows no recent volatility but price is trending, model should not assume continuation — expect mean reversion or sideways correction.
- When sentiment is negative and price is rising, model should reduce forecasted upside; avoid “sentiment-driven” overcorrection.
- If model forecasts a sharp peak followed by steep decline, check for lag — true price often lags model by 2–3 days in downward moves.
- For 30-day forecasts, if model consistently overestimates by 3–5% in the last 5–7 days, apply a 1–2% downward correction to final 7–10 days.
